title: Make the comparison visible.
dek: Two highlighted rows still ask the listener to search through a page of numbers.

before.title: The full table
before.alt: Original table with 22 commuting zones and four numeric columns. North Hickory and Raleigh-Cary are highlighted.
before.label: REGIONAL COMPARISON · 2000

after.title: Two exposed regions had very different workforces.
after.note: Year 2000 · descriptive comparison
after.cue: These two places both faced import competition, but their initial workforces looked quite different.
after.label: REGIONAL COMPARISON · 2000
after.alt: Year 2000: North Hickory, NC has manufacturing employment share 43.0%, BA share of ages 18–64 15.6%, population 377.5 thousand. Raleigh-Cary, NC: 17.0%, 34.2%, and 1,420.0 thousand. Import-penetration change, 2000–2012: 4.40 and 3.42 percentage points, respectively.

diagnosis: The original already tells us which two rows matter. A revision can carry that emphasis through to the comparison itself.
changes: Keep the two highlighted places together.
Use a common scale for each pair of percentages.
Keep population and exposure in a separate context line.
preserved: All eight numbers for the highlighted regions, with their dates and units.
deferred: The other 20 regions remain in the original and in the complete data download below.
practice: Write down the comparison you intend to say aloud. Make that comparison the figure; keep the full table available.
principle: Minimize tables with lots of numbers!
context: The source highlights these same two regions; the revision develops that comparison.

title: Give the model a reason to exist.
dek: Put the policy question before the payoff function.

before.title: First build · PDF p. 2
before.alt: The first content slide presents investment payoffs and a network-dependent marginal return.
before.label: THE POLICY QUESTION

before.title: Later build · PDF p. 4
before.alt: The same slide adds a targeting question below the payoff and verbal interpretation.
before.label: THE POLICY QUESTION

after.title: Whose incentives should a planner change?
lines: An investment changes other people’s incentives.
A planner changes incentives to raise total welfare within a limited budget.
after.note: Schematic network · strategic complements
after.cue: Changing one person’s incentives can also change what others do. Whose incentives should the planner change?
after.label: THE POLICY QUESTION
after.alt: Schematic five-person network. B is highlighted as a possible intervention target.

after.title: Now give that question a model.
after.note: The planner changes \(b\) at a cost. The full targeting problem follows.
after.cue: This payoff formalizes the direct incentive and the response to neighbors.
after.label: THE POLICY QUESTION

diagnosis: The policy question appears only after the audience has encountered the mathematical setup. A short opening can reverse that dependency.
changes: Name the planner’s decision first.
Use an illustrative network to give spillovers a meaning.
Introduce the original payoff once it answers a known question.
preserved: The source’s payoff, simultaneous choices, and distinction between complements and substitutes.
deferred: The formal targeting problem, quadratic intervention cost, symmetry, and equilibrium assumptions follow in the model section.
practice: Before your first model slide, write one sentence saying what decision the model will help us understand.
context: The original already builds gradually and labels terms. This repair changes the order. The comparison shows the first and final builds; intermediate PDF page 3 is omitted.
beforeCaption: Original first and final builds. PDF pp. 2 and 4; p. 3 omitted.

title: Put the meaning next to the symbol.
dek: A notation key should be where the listener needs it.

before.title: Exposure equation · PDF p. 17
before.alt: Three exposure formulas with time subscripts and no adjacent key for M, L, or output growth.
before.label: LOCAL ROBOT EXPOSURE

after.title: Use old industry shares to predict local robot exposure.
lines: \(E_c\): predicted exposure in local labor market \(c\)
after.note: Instrument for measured US exposure; time indices omitted here.
after.cue: Start with the industries a place had before widespread robot adoption, then weight European penetration in those same industries.
after.label: LOCAL ROBOT EXPOSURE

after.title: “Adjusted” removes an output-growth component.
lines: \(g^Y\): industry output growth over the period
\(0\) and \(t\): beginning and end of the period
after.note: Industry indices omitted. Causal interpretation requires instrument-validity assumptions.
after.cue: The adjustment separates robot-stock growth per initial worker from the part attributed to industry output growth.
after.label: LOCAL ROBOT EXPOSURE

diagnosis: The page already explains European adoption and the 1970 weights. Its formulas still ask the audience to retrieve several symbols from elsewhere.
changes: Teach the weighted sum in words.
Attach a local key to the same expression.
Explain the adjustment on a second build.
preserved: The weighted exposure construction, 1970 baseline, European instrument, and output-growth adjustment.
deferred: The US exposure formula stays in the source. Suppressing indices is disclosed; validity is not inferred from the instrument’s construction.
practice: Cover every slide except the one on screen. Can a listener recover what each load-bearing symbol means?
context: The source defines the European comparison and 1970 weights. The revision adds a local notation key.

title: Give the method a job before its formula.
dek: An example gives the audience a question for the method to answer.

before.title: Objective · PDF p. 17
before.alt: LASSO objective followed by a general norm definition.
before.label: EARNINGS PREDICTION

before.title: Example · PDF p. 33
before.alt: Earnings prediction example with OLS and LASSO test errors.
before.label: EARNINGS PREDICTION

after.title: LASSO has lower test error in this earnings example.
after.note: 1978 earnings · 15,992 people · 7,996 training. Outcome units are not specified on the example slide.
after.cue: Here is a concrete prediction problem. Why might a penalized fit do better on new observations?
after.label: EARNINGS PREDICTION
after.alt: Test root-mean-squared prediction error, lower is better: OLS 1.4093; LASSO 0.7379. Both bars start at zero.

after.title: A penalty can leave fewer predictors.
after.note: Selection is about prediction; it does not identify causal effects.
after.cue: The penalty can set some coefficients to zero. These counts describe this particular fit.
after.label: EARNINGS PREDICTION

after.title: Balance fit against coefficient size.
lines: First sum: fit to the training sample
Second term: penalty on absolute coefficients
after.note: Assess prediction on observations outside the training sample.
after.cue: Now the objective describes the tradeoff we have just seen.
after.label: EARNINGS PREDICTION

diagnosis: Within this subsection, the concrete example follows the formula. Moving it forward gives a broader audience a specific problem to think about.
changes: Preview the observed comparison.
Explain what the penalty does.
Show the objective with labels.
preserved: The two reported test errors, feature counts, and L1-penalized objective.
deferred: Intervening lecture material remains in the source. The example reports prediction errors without uncertainty estimates.
practice: Find one honest example that makes your first formula worth understanding. Put it before the formula.
context: NBER lecture. Earlier slides motivate prediction and regularization; this revision changes the order within the LASSO subsection.
beforeCaption: Selected milestones in source order; intervening slides omitted.
values: Reported test root-mean-squared error: OLS 1.4093; LASSO 0.7379. Lower is better.
The source’s outcome scale is retained. The original example does not specify units or report uncertainty.

title: Teach the visual alphabet first.
dek: Six unfamiliar diagrams are easier to read after one has been explained.

before.title: Matrix first · PDF p. 11
before.alt: The source introduces the eigenvalue decomposition.
before.label: PATTERNS ON A NETWORK

before.title: Six patterns · PDF p. 12
before.alt: Six ring-network patterns appear together; signs and sizes have no written key on this page.
before.label: PATTERNS ON A NETWORK

after.title: Begin with a pattern everyone can read.
lines: Each dot is one node on the ring.
The + sign denotes a positive entry.
after.note: Equal dot sizes mean equal magnitudes; sign and size encode vector entries.
after.cue: Read the entries as a pattern across the same network.
after.label: PATTERNS ON A NETWORK
after.alt: A fourteen-node ring. All entries are positive and equal in magnitude.

after.title: Neighbors can move in opposite directions.
lines: Every entry has the same magnitude.
after.note: The source’s two extreme patterns; same ring, different entries.
after.cue: Now the pattern alternates. The network has not changed; the entries have.
after.label: PATTERNS ON A NETWORK
after.alt: The same fourteen-node ring. Plus and minus entries alternate; all magnitudes are equal.

after.title: The network preserves these patterns up to a multiplier.
after.note: \(u\): pattern · \(g\): network · \(\lambda\): multiplier. Intermediate patterns stay in the full source.
after.cue: These are eigenvectors: applying the network rescales the same pattern.
after.label: PATTERNS ON A NETWORK
after.alt: The common and alternating patterns, side by side on the same fourteen-node ring. Applying the network rescales each pattern.

diagnosis: The source stages the matrix before the pictures. The next build adds six patterns without a written key for the visual encoding.
changes: Explain one pattern before comparing several.
Use signs as well as color.
Name the mathematical object after its operation is visible.
preserved: The ring and its two extreme patterns. The simplification changes the teaching sequence, not the decomposition.
deferred: Intermediate patterns and the full matrix identity remain in the original.
practice: Introduce the meaning of one mark before asking your audience to compare a whole collection of marks.
context: The original has animation builds. This revision extends that approach by staging the newly introduced patterns and adding a visible key.
beforeCaption: Actual source page; original aspect ratio preserved.

title: Draw the estimates—and the uncertainty.
dek: A coefficient plot should preserve the inconvenient results too.

before.title: Regression table · PDF p. 76
before.alt: A six-column table reports current-exposure estimates and pre-period placebo estimates with standard errors.
before.label: TRADE & EMPLOYMENT

after.title: Show current and future exposure separately.
after.note: 10-year-equivalent manufacturing employment / population change. Approx. 95% intervals; state-clustered SE; population-weighted.
after.cue: Read the upper three as current-exposure estimates, and the lower three as placebo comparisons using future exposure.
after.label: TRADE & EMPLOYMENT

diagnosis: The highlighted table contains two different comparisons. A single plot can preserve all six estimates while making the grouping and precision easier to see.
changes: Keep current-exposure and future-exposure rows separate.
Reconstruct intervals transparently from the reported standard errors.
Retain the positive 1970–80 placebo coefficient.
preserved: All six coefficients and standard errors. Outcome: ten times the annual change in manufacturing employment / working-age population, in percentage points; exposure: $1,000 per worker.
deferred: Full table notes remain in the original. N = 722 per period, 1,444 in pooled columns; state-clustered SE and population weights apply. Normal-approximation intervals are a new display, not reported intervals.
practice: Decide which coefficients answer your claim. Plot every one needed for that claim, including the awkward ones.
principle: Minimize tables with lots of numbers!
context: A 2026 graduate lecture reproducing a table from Autor, Dorn, and Hanson (2013). The positive 1970–80 placebo coefficient is retained.
values: Intervals use estimate ± 1.96 × SE. Axis units: outcome percentage points per $1,000 exposure per worker.

title: Let the title carry the finding.
dek: “Results” names a section. It does not tell the room what happened.

after.title: Pupils offered tutoring scored higher.
after.note: Illustrative randomized pilot · 300 pupils · 95% CI
after.cue: This is the effect of being offered tutoring in this pilot. The estimate is 0.18 standard deviations, not an attendance effect.
after.label: TUTORING PILOT
after.alt: Effect of a tutoring offer: +0.18 standard deviations; illustrative 95% confidence interval +0.06 to +0.30. Zero is marked on the axis.

diagnosis: The original contains the answer, but asks the listener to translate notation into a finding while also reading the design details.
changes: State the finding in ordinary words.
Give the estimate a labeled scale and interval.
Keep “offered” in the claim to preserve the estimand.
preserved: The invented offer effect, confidence interval, randomized design, sample size, and outcome units.
deferred: Design and estimation details follow. The estimate concerns an offer in this pilot; attendance and generalization require further evidence.
practice: Read your slide titles aloud without their bodies. Do they say what your audience should remember?
context: Fictional randomized tutoring pilot, also used in case 12.
values: Illustrative offer effect: 0.18 standard deviations; illustrative 95% CI [0.06, 0.30].
Fictional design: 150 pupils offered tutoring, 150 not offered; 300 in total.

title: Let two people teach the general case.
dek: A listener should see what the matrix counts before seeing its inverse.

after.title: Each response feeds back to the other.
lines: Each receives \(\tfrac14\) of the other’s total response
after.note: Toy model · symmetric players
after.cue: Each starts with one unit. Each also receives one quarter of the other’s response.
after.label: A NETWORK RESPONSE MODEL
after.alt: Two people A and B, each with a direct effect of 1. Each total includes one quarter of the other person’s total response.

after.title: Each round contributes less.
after.note: For each person: \(a=1+\tfrac14a\), hence \(a=\tfrac43\).
after.cue: The first round adds a quarter, the next a sixteenth. The total converges to four thirds.
after.label: A NETWORK RESPONSE MODEL
after.alt: Successive contributions: direct 1, first round 0.25, second 0.0625, third 0.015625. Cumulative responses approach 4/3.

after.title: The general formula counts the same rounds.
after.note: Nonnegative \(G\) and \(\beta\). The spectral-radius condition ensures repeated feedback dies out.
after.cue: Now each term has a job we recognize. The convergence condition is still essential.
after.label: A NETWORK RESPONSE MODEL

diagnosis: The original starts with the answer in its most general form. The listener has to specialize it before understanding the mechanism.
changes: Solve a small case with the mechanism intact.
Show the contribution of each round.
Carry the interpretation into the general notation.
preserved: The response equation and convergence condition. In the toy case, \(\frac{1}{1-1/4}=\frac43\) exactly.
deferred: Other network structures and parameter values. The convergence condition remains necessary.
practice: Find the smallest example in which your main force still operates. Teach it, then say exactly what generalizes.
context: Constructed model: two people, direct effect 1, reciprocal spillover ¼.

title: Replace the section break with a bridge.
dek: Help the person who missed the last five slides rejoin the argument.

before.title: Moment conditions
before.note: The transition assumes the audience remembers the model’s purpose.
before.label: THE ARGUMENT SO FAR

after.title: The model gives us one demand equation.
lines: Now we need to separate low price sensitivity from limited attention to price changes.
after.note: Electricity-demand example from the essay
after.cue: We have finished the model. The one thing we carry forward is a demand equation. Now we need to separate price sensitivity from attention.
after.label: THE ARGUMENT SO FAR

after.title: Keep returning to the main argument.
after.note: Five re-entry points distributed through the talk.
after.cue: At each stop, repeat what the details have established and what we will use next.
after.label: THE ARGUMENT SO FAR

diagnosis: A highlighted outline locates the speaker without restoring the argument. The next technical slide still depends on uninterrupted attention.
changes: Say what the last section produced.
Name the one object carried forward.
Explain the next obstacle before its technical treatment.
preserved: The move from behavior to a demand equation and then estimation. The bridge supplements the technical section.
deferred: The moment conditions follow with definitions at use.
practice: After each technical block, write two sentences for someone returning to the room: what we have, and why the next step matters.
principle: Give people a way back in
context: Based on the essay’s fictional electricity-demand example.

title: Build the short route before you need it.
dek: Questions should change the amount of detail, not whether the room hears the result.

before.title: A fixed route has no room to contract.
before.note: Rehearsal plan · 68 speaking minutes before questions.
before.label: A 75-MINUTE SEMINAR
before.alt: Introduction 8, model 15, data 12, results 20, implications 8, conclusion 5 speaking minutes; total 68.

after.title: Prepare two routes to the same result.
after.note: Normal route: 53 minutes · short route: 47 minutes.
after.cue: I will give the model and data at a high level, then show the main result. The details are available for discussion.
after.label: A 75-MINUTE SEMINAR
after.alt: Normal route: 8, 9, 6, 17, 8, 5 minutes, total 53. Short route: 8, 6, 3, 17, 8, 5, total 47.

after.title: A short version must still say something.
after.note: Policy predictions rely on the model’s assumed attention rule remaining applicable.
after.cue: Keep the input, output, and relevant limitation visible when the intervening machinery contracts.
after.label: A 75-MINUTE SEMINAR

diagnosis: The fixed plan makes every setup slide mandatory. Twelve minutes of early questions then push the first result to minute 47.
changes: Protect time for the result and implications.
Rehearse actual shorter model and data explanations.
Use a contingency appropriate to the time already spent.
preserved: The core contribution and the essay’s approximate 35- and 60-minute landmarks for a long job talk.
deferred: Detailed model and data exposition contracts. The scenarios assume all added question time occurs before results; later interruptions would require more choices.
practice: Build a core of roughly twenty distinct displays, with optional branches. Count animation builds as one display. Rehearse both routes aloud.
principle: Set deadlines and adjust as you go
context: Constructed rehearsal plan; early-question time is added before the main results.
values: Fixed speaking minutes: introduction 8, model 15, data 12, results 20, implications 8, conclusion 5 = 68.
With 12 minutes of early questions, normal results start at 35; with 18, short-route results start at 35. Both finish implications at 60 and conclusion at 65.

title: Give the audience the axes first.
dek: A complete diagram can be the destination rather than the starting point.

before.title: Comparative statics
before.label: A DEMAND INCREASE
before.alt: The new intersection is above and to the right of the original. Price rises from P0 to P1 and quantity from Q0 to Q1.

after.title: First, say what the axes measure.
after.note: Schematic market: price vertically; quantity horizontally.
after.cue: The vertical axis is price, and the horizontal axis is quantity.
after.label: A DEMAND INCREASE
after.alt: Price on the vertical axis; quantity on the horizontal axis.

after.title: Locate the initial market outcome.
after.note: Supply rises; initial demand falls. Their intersection is the initial outcome.
after.cue: Begin with supply and the original demand curve. Their intersection gives our starting point.
after.label: A DEMAND INCREASE
after.alt: Upward supply and downward initial demand meet at the starting equilibrium.

after.title: Now shift demand.
after.note: Higher demand at every price; supply held fixed. Illustrative shift only.
after.cue: The new curve means buyers demand more at any given price. Supply has not changed.
after.label: A DEMAND INCREASE
after.alt: Demand shifts outward while supply stays fixed.

after.title: Trace the change back to the axes.
after.note: In this schematic, both equilibrium price and quantity rise.
after.cue: The new intersection is up and to the right, so price and quantity both rise.
after.label: A DEMAND INCREASE
after.alt: The new intersection is above and to the right of the original. Price rises from P0 to P1 and quantity from Q0 to Q1.

diagnosis: When the axes, curves, shift, and projections appear together, the listener has to decide where to start while the speaker is already interpreting the outcome.
changes: Explain the axes before adding curves.
Establish the baseline before changing it.
Only then trace the implication.
preserved: The same final diagram and comparative-static reasoning. The improvement is the route through it, not fewer final marks.
deferred: The final diagram stays intact. The sequence gives each part an explanation.
practice: Put up only the axes. Explain them. Add one economically meaningful object at a time.

title: Give the claim a boundary, not an apology.
dek: A credible limitation should help the audience understand the result’s scope.

before.title: Caveats
before.note: Fictional tutoring pilot; the result itself is not on this slide.
before.label: FINDING & SCOPE

after.title: The offer helped in this pilot. Scaling is a separate question.

items.title: What we learn
items.text: An offer raised short-run scores by 0.18 SD in this fictional district; 95% CI 0.06–0.30.

items.title: What we do not learn
items.text: Attendance effects, persistence, or effects in other districts and at national scale.

items.title: What comes next
items.text: Test whether staffing and participation change at larger scale.

after.note: Fictional tutoring pilot · randomized offers · 300 pupils
after.cue: This design answers the offer question here. A larger rollout could change staffing and participation, and would need new evidence.
after.label: FINDING & SCOPE

diagnosis: The caveats are sensible, but without the finding there is no claim for them to qualify. The audience hears reservations before it knows what was accomplished.
changes: State one proportionate finding.
Name a concrete limit to its interpretation.
Explain the next research task without claiming to have done it.
preserved: The same illustrative offer effect and uncertainty, with limits on attendance and generalization.
deferred: The limitations remain on the slide, after the finding they qualify.
practice: Write “What this establishes” and “What it leaves open” in equally plain language. Check both with your advisor.
context: The same fictional tutoring pilot as case 07.
